sceneHappening: Malta, the road to Rome, and Paul preaching under guard
summary: When we have escaped, we then learn that the island is called Malta. The foreign people show us uncommon kindness, for they kindle a fire and receive us all, because of the present rain and because of the cold. When Paul has gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper comes out because of the heat and fastens on his hand. When the foreigners see the creature hanging from his hand, they say to one another, "No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed to live." However he shakes off the creature into the fire and suffers no harm. But they expect that he will have swollen or fallen down dead suddenly. But when they have looked for a long time and see nothing unusual happen to him, they change their minds and say that he is a god. In the neighborhood of that place are lands belonging to the chief man of the island, whose name is Publius, who receives us and entertains us courteously for three days. The father of Publius lies sick of fever and dysentery, and Paul enters in to him and prays, and laying his hands on him, heals him. After this the rest also who have diseases in the island come and are cured. They also honor us with many honors, and when we sail, they put on board whatever we need. After three months we set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered in the island, whose sign was The Twin Brothers. Touching at Syracuse, we stay there three days. From there we circle around and arrive at Rhegium, and after one day a south wind blows, and on the second day we come to Puteoli, where we find brothers, and are invited to stay with them seven days. So we come to Rome. From there the brothers, when they hear of us, come to meet us as far as the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. When Paul sees them, he thanks God and takes courage. When we enter into Rome, Paul is allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guards him. After three days he calls together those who are the leaders of the Jews, and when they have come together, he says to them, "I, brothers, though I had done nothing against the people, or the customs of our fathers, still was delivered prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans, who, when they had examined me, desired to set me free, because there was no cause of death in me. But when the Jews spoke against it, I was constrained to appeal to Caesar, not that I had anything about which to accuse my nation. For this cause therefore I asked to see you and to speak with you, for because of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain." They say to him, "We neither received letters from Judea concerning you, nor did any of the brothers come here and report or speak any evil of you. But we desire to hear from you what you think, for as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against." When they have appointed him a day, many come to him at his lodging, to whom he explains, testifying about the Kingdom of God, and persuading them concerning Jesus, both from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening. Some believe the things which are spoken, and some disbelieve. When they don't agree among themselves, they depart after Paul has spoken one word: "The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying, 'Go to this people, and say, in hearing you will hear, and will in no way understand; and in seeing you will see, and will in no way perceive: for this people's heart has grown callous, their ears are dull of hearing, and they have closed their eyes; or else perhaps they might perceive with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again, and I would heal them.' Be it known therefore to you, that this salvation of God is sent to the Gentiles. They will also listen." Paul stays two whole years in his own rented dwelling, and welcomes all who come to him, preaching the Kingdom of God, and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.
whySettingMatters: Malta lies about sixty miles south of Sicily, and a traditional site in St. Paul's Bay fits Luke's description of a bay and a beach with a reef (27:39-41). Luke calls the Maltese "foreigners" (barbaroi), a Greek term for non-Greek speakers, and they treat the shipwreck survivors with unusual kindness (philanthrōpia). The snake bite and the people's change of mind recall Lystra (14:11-18), where Paul was first taken for a god and then stoned. "Justice" (Dikē) is a Greek goddess, and the islanders think she has caught up with him. Publius is called "chief man" (prōtos), a title found in inscriptions from Malta. The Alexandrian ship with "Twin Brothers" (Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri) as its figurehead, protectors of sailors, shows how much of the ancient world lived with pagan symbols. Puteoli was the main port for the Egyptian grain trade; Appii Forum and Three Taverns were stations on the Appian Way, about 43 and 33 miles from Rome. The believers in Rome had heard of Paul from his letter to the Romans, and their meeting him is a high moment. Paul is under house arrest, chained to a soldier. His closing quotation from Isaiah 6:9-10 echoes the end of Jesus' parable of the sower, and "this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles" sets up the final note. Acts ends abruptly, two years into the house arrest, without saying what happened to Paul at trial; why Luke stops there is debated (whether the book was written then, or whether the story's point was reached). Tradition says Paul was later executed in Rome under Nero, in about AD 64 to 67. The last word of the book in Greek is "unhindered" (akōlytōs), and the story it tells runs from Jerusalem to the center of the empire, with the word of God still going out.

questions: The islanders' first and second judgments about Paul are both wrong. What does Luke say about how people read the signs?
Paul greets the Roman believers, and takes courage. What does that scene tell you about what he needed?
Paul quotes Isaiah 6 and says the salvation of God has gone to the Gentiles. How does that sentence close one thing and open another?
Acts ends with "without hindrance." Why do you think Luke stops there?
